title: Binary search
held: find a target by halving a sorted range
body: Keep an interval containing every possible match. Compare its middle item and discard the impossible half. The input must already be sorted.
cost: O(log n) comparisons and O(1) extra space.
mistake: An unsorted input invalidates the search invariant.

title: Linear search
held: inspect each element until it matches
body: Inspect elements in order until a match is found or the input ends. No sorting precondition is needed.
cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
example: Scan [8,2,9] for 2: compare 8, then 2.
mistake: Sorting first can cost more than a single scan.

title: Merge sort
held: split a list then combine sorted halves
body: Recursively sort two halves, then merge by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. Taking from the left on equality preserves stability.
cost: O(n log n) time; typically O(n) auxiliary array storage.
mistake: Repeatedly rescanning a prefix makes a merge unnecessarily expensive.

title: Quicksort
held: partition a list around a chosen pivot
body: Choose a pivot, partition by comparison with it, and recursively sort the parts. Three-way partitioning handles duplicate keys well.
cost: Expected O(n log n) with randomized pivots; O(n²) worst case.
example: Partition [4,1,4,8,2] into values below, equal to, and above 4.
mistake: Repeatedly choosing an extreme pivot can make the algorithm quadratic.

title: Heapsort
held: remove the maximum repeatedly from a binary heap
body: Build a max heap, swap its maximum to the end, and restore the heap in the shrinking prefix.
cost: O(n log n) time; O(1) auxiliary space in-place.
example: The heap root gives the largest remaining element.
mistake: Heapsort is generally not stable.

title: Insertion sort
held: move each item into its place in the sorted prefix
body: Maintain a sorted prefix and shift larger items right to insert the next one. Useful for small or nearly sorted inputs.
cost: O(n²) worst case; O(n) on sorted inputs; O(1) extra space.
mistake: Worst-case asymptotics alone do not determine speed on small inputs.

title: Counting sort
held: sort integer keys by counting occurrences
body: Count each integer key, then reconstruct sorted output. A cumulative-count variant preserves record stability.
cost: O(n+k) time for key range size k; O(k) counts.
mistake: A huge sparse key range makes the array impractical.

title: Radix sort
held: sort keys one digit at a time
body: Process key digits in stable passes. Least-significant-digit sorting relies on preserving the order established by earlier passes.
cost: O(d(n+b)) for d digits and radix b.
example: Sort nonnegative fixed-width integers by successive bytes.
mistake: An unstable pass breaks the usual LSD algorithm.

title: Breadth-first search
held: visit graph vertices in distance layers
body: A FIFO queue explores vertices by increasing edge count. Mark a vertex when enqueuing it. Parent links reconstruct a shortest unweighted path.
cost: O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary space.
example: bfs A D: A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D
mistake: BFS does not minimize arbitrary weighted distances.

title: Depth-first search
held: follow a graph branch before backtracking
body: Explore one branch at a time using recursion or a stack. Discovery and finishing information helps analyze cycles and components.
cost: O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary space.
example: Explore one branch to its end before trying another neighbor.
mistake: A visited flag differs from an active recursion-stack flag.

title: Dijkstra's algorithm
held: settle the closest unsettled vertex with nonnegative edges
body: Remove the smallest tentative distance from a priority queue and relax its outgoing edges. Nonnegative weights justify finalizing that distance.
cost: O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap.
example: dijkstra A D: A-B:4, A-C:1, C-B:2, B-D:1
mistake: Negative edges invalidate standard finalization.

title: Bellman-Ford
held: relax every edge repeatedly to handle negative weights
body: Relax all edges up to V-1 times. An additional reachable improvement indicates a reachable negative cycle.
cost: O(VE) time and O(V) distance storage.
example: A negative edge can coexist with well-defined shortest paths.
mistake: A negative edge is not itself a negative cycle.

title: Floyd-Warshall
held: allow each vertex as an intermediate in a distance matrix
body: For each intermediate vertex k, improve d[i,j] with d[i,k]+d[k,j]. A negative diagonal afterward indicates a negative cycle.
cost: O(V³) time and O(V²) memory.
example: Each iteration expands the set of allowed intermediate vertices.
mistake: The k loop must be outermost for the standard invariant.

title: A star search
held: guide path finding with a lower bound estimate
body: Order nodes by path cost g plus heuristic h. Admissible h never overestimates remaining cost; consistency supports closing nodes without reopening.
cost: Cost depends on the graph and heuristic; worst-case search can be large.
example: Manhattan distance bounds remaining unit-cost movement on a four-neighbor grid.
mistake: An overestimating heuristic can lose optimality.

title: Topological sorting
held: order tasks so every prerequisite comes first
body: Repeatedly remove an indegree-zero vertex and decrease its successors' indegrees. Remaining vertices after the queue empties indicate a cycle.
cost: O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary space.
example: toposort: plan-build, build-test, test-release
mistake: A cyclic directed graph has no topological ordering.

title: Kruskal's algorithm
held: connect components using the lightest safe edge
body: Sort undirected edges by weight and accept an edge only when it joins separate components. Union-find tests connectivity efficiently.
cost: O(E log E), dominated by sorting.
example: An undirected spanning tree connects all vertices with V-1 edges.
mistake: An MST minimizes total tree weight, not every pairwise path.

title: Prim's algorithm
held: grow a tree by its lightest outgoing edge
body: Start at a vertex and repeatedly select the lightest edge crossing from the tree to an outside vertex. Restart to cover disconnected components.
cost: O(E log V) with a binary heap.
example: The cut property justifies the selected edge.
mistake: Disconnected graphs need a spanning forest.

title: Union-find
held: track which elements share a connected component
body: Represent each set by a root. Union by rank or size limits growth; path compression shortens later finds.
cost: Amortized O(α(n)) per operation with both optimizations.
example: Union A-B then B-C makes A and C share a representative.
mistake: Standard union-find does not support arbitrary edge deletions.

title: Strongly connected components
held: find directed regions with mutual reachability
body: Partition a directed graph into maximal groups where every member reaches every other. Contracting the groups produces a DAG.
cost: O(V+E) for Tarjan or Kosaraju.
example: A→B→C→A is one strongly connected component.
mistake: Undirected connectivity is a different property.

title: Maximum flow
held: send the greatest flow through a capacity network
body: Maintain capacities and flow conservation. Residual edges record where flow can be added or undone. Augment until no residual source-to-sink path remains.
cost: Edmonds-Karp: O(VE²).
example: Reverse residual edges allow an earlier routing decision to be revised.
mistake: Removing reverse edges can prevent reaching the optimum.

title: Bipartite matching
held: pair vertices across two sets without reusing any vertex
body: An augmenting path alternates unused and used edges. Flipping it increases the matching size by one.
cost: Hopcroft-Karp: O(E√V).
example: Match workers to compatible jobs, one job per worker.
mistake: Greedy pairing need not maximize the number of pairs.

title: Dynamic programming
held: store solutions to repeated smaller problems
body: Define sufficient state, a recurrence, and base cases. Reuse solutions instead of recomputing them.
cost: Roughly states times transitions examined per state.
example: Edit distance stores solutions for pairs of prefixes.
mistake: Memoization cannot repair a recurrence that omits necessary state.

title: Greedy algorithms
held: make the best immediate choice without reconsidering it
body: Choose the locally best feasible step. Correctness requires structure, often an exchange argument or cut property.
cost: Depends on the algorithm; sorting often dominates.
example: Earliest-finishing interval selection maximizes the count of compatible intervals.
mistake: Largest-coin-first fails for coins 1,3,4 and amount 6.

title: Backtracking
held: try a choice and undo it when it cannot reach a solution
body: Build partial solutions, prune invalid ones, and explore the remaining choices. The partial-state invariant justifies pruning.
cost: Often exponential in the number of choices.
example: Assign a legal Sudoku digit and undo unsuccessful choices.
mistake: Pruning merely unlikely branches can remove the only solution.

title: Branch and bound
held: discard a branch when its optimistic bound cannot beat the incumbent
body: Keep the best feasible solution. Bound each unfinished branch and discard it when even its optimistic outcome cannot improve the incumbent.
cost: Worst-case exponential.
example: For maximization, prune when the upper bound is no greater than the incumbent.
mistake: A bound in the wrong direction can remove the optimum.

title: Zero-one knapsack
held: choose indivisible items under a weight capacity
body: For each item and capacity, choose between skipping it and taking it once. Update a one-dimensional capacity table downward to prevent reuse.
cost: O(nC) time and O(C) memory; pseudo-polynomial in capacity C.
mistake: Updating capacities upward permits unbounded item reuse.

title: Coin change
held: make an amount with the fewest reusable denominations
body: Let dp[a] be the minimum coins for amount a. Try dp[a-c]+1 for each coin c. Keep unreachable amounts explicitly unreachable.
cost: O(AC) for amount A and C denominations.
example: coins 6 with [1,3,4]
mistake: Greedy change is not valid for every coin system.

title: Edit distance
held: count insertions deletions and substitutions between strings
body: Use a table over prefix pairs. Each cell chooses deletion, insertion, or substitution; equal characters allow free diagonal progress.
cost: O(mn) time; O(min(m,n)) space for only the distance.
example: edit kitten -> sitting
mistake: Operation distance is not semantic difference.

title: Longest common subsequence
held: find the longest ordered sequence shared by two strings
body: If final characters match, extend the shorter-prefix solution. Otherwise choose the better result from dropping either final character.
cost: O(mn) with a prefix table.
example: lcs ABCBDAB / BDCABA
mistake: Subsequences need not be contiguous; substrings must be.

title: Longest increasing subsequence
held: keep the smallest tail for each possible increasing length
body: Maintain the smallest possible ending value for each increasing subsequence length. Binary search finds which tail a value improves.
cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) memory.
mistake: Strictly increasing and nondecreasing need different equality rules.

title: Interval scheduling
held: choose the largest set of compatible time intervals
body: Sort by finish time and select each next interval starting after the previous selected one ends. An exchange argument proves the equal-value case.
cost: O(n log n), dominated by sorting.
example: Select meetings by earliest finish time.
mistake: Weighted interval scheduling generally needs dynamic programming.

title: Hash tables
held: map keys into buckets and resolve collisions
body: Hash a key to a bucket, then compare keys to resolve collisions. Manage the load and resizing policy.
cost: Expected O(1) operations under suitable assumptions; O(n) worst case.
example: Store the latest value associated with an exact key.
mistake: Equal hashes do not imply equal keys.

title: Priority queues
held: retrieve the smallest item while new items arrive
body: A min heap keeps each parent no greater than its children. It supports insertion and removal of the minimum.
cost: O(log n) insert/remove, O(1) peek, O(n) bottom-up build.
example: Dijkstra queues tentative distances.
mistake: The heap's array is not globally sorted.

title: Tries
held: follow characters through a tree to locate a prefix
body: Store paths for keys and share common prefixes. Mark complete words separately from internal prefix nodes.
cost: O(k) lookup for k characters with constant-time child access.
example: car, cart, and cat share ca.
mistake: An existing prefix need not be a complete stored word.

title: Binary search trees
held: organize ordered keys in smaller and larger subtrees
body: Search follows one branch per comparison. Balanced variants maintain height bounds with rotations or other restructuring.
cost: O(h) for height h; O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed.
example: In-order traversal returns sorted keys.
mistake: Ordinary search trees are not automatically balanced.

title: Stacks and queues
held: contrast last in first out with first in first out
body: Stacks remove the newest item; queues remove the oldest. They support depth-first and breadth-first work respectively.
cost: O(1) amortized endpoint operations with appropriate implementations.
example: Undo uses a stack; BFS uses a queue.
mistake: Shifting an array to remove its first item costs O(n).

title: Fenwick trees
held: update array values and query prefix sums efficiently
body: Store selected partial sums and jump between ranges using the lowest set bit.
cost: O(log n) updates and queries; O(n) memory.
example: Range sum is the difference of two prefix sums.
mistake: One-based indexing formulas cannot be copied unchanged to zero-based storage.

title: Segment trees
held: combine summaries of intervals in a balanced tree
body: Each node summarizes an interval. Combine fully covered nodes during a query and update nodes on the affected leaf's path.
cost: O(log n) point updates and range queries; O(n) memory.
example: Store range minima or sums.
mistake: The combine operation must be associative.

title: Bloom filters
held: test membership with possible false positives
body: Insertion sets several hash-selected bits. A zero proves absence; all ones indicate possible presence.
cost: O(k) for k hashes with a fixed bit array.
example: Skip expensive lookups when the filter proves absence.
mistake: Naively clearing bits on deletion can create false negatives.

title: Knuth-Morris-Pratt
held: reuse matched prefixes while searching for a pattern
body: Precompute how much pattern remains matched after a mismatch. Search does not back up the text pointer.
cost: O(n+m) time and O(m) extra space.
example: Handle repeated-prefix patterns without rescanning text.
mistake: Resetting the match length to zero loses the optimization.

title: Rabin-Karp
held: roll a fingerprint over consecutive text windows
body: Compare a rolling window hash to the pattern's hash. Verify characters on matches to handle collisions.
cost: Expected linear behavior in suitable settings; O(nm) worst case.
example: Slide a fixed-width search window through text.
mistake: Hash equality alone is not an exact substring proof.

title: Euclidean algorithm
held: replace a pair with the smaller number and its remainder
body: Repeatedly replace (a,b) with (b,a mod b) until b is zero. Common divisors are preserved.
cost: O(log min(a,b)) remainder steps for positive inputs.
mistake: This demo defines gcd(0,0)=0 and normalizes signs.

title: Prime sieve
held: mark multiples to enumerate primes below a bound
body: For each unmarked prime p through √n, mark multiples starting at p². Remaining numbers from 2 are primes.
cost: O(n log log n) time and O(n) marker space.
example: primes 100
mistake: The integer 1 is not prime.

title: Modular arithmetic
held: calculate remainders under a positive modulus
body: Repeated squaring computes powers modulo m without constructing the full power. Arithmetic is over residue classes.
cost: O(log e) modular multiplications for exponent e.
example: powmod 7 128 13
mistake: Division requires an inverse, which exists only for a divisor coprime to m.

title: Algorithmic complexity
held: describe resource growth as input size increases
body: Big O bounds growth under a cost model. Distinguish worst-case, expected, and amortized statements and specify the input parameter.
cost: Examples: O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2^n).
example: Doubling n roughly quadruples n² but adds one to log₂ n.
mistake: Asymptotic bounds alone do not predict a particular small run's speed.

title: NP completeness
held: classify problems using polynomial time reductions
body: NP problems have polynomial-time verifiable certificates. NP-complete problems are in NP and as hard as every NP problem under polynomial reductions.
cost: No polynomial-time algorithm for all NP-complete problems is known.
example: Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete.
mistake: NP does not mean not polynomial; NP-hard need not imply membership in NP.

title: Loop invariants
held: state what remains true before and after every loop step
body: Show initialization, preservation by a step, and usefulness at termination. Partial correctness alone does not establish termination.
cost: Proof effort depends on the model and property.
example: Binary search keeps every possible match inside its remaining interval.
mistake: Sample executions do not prove every execution.

title: Functional core imperative shell
held: separate deterministic decisions from external effects
body: Put decisions in pure functions over explicit inputs. Keep persistence, clocks, and network effects in a shell so decisions can be replayed.
cost: A design boundary, not a complexity bound.
example: A transition returns next state and requested effects; the shell performs them.
mistake: Purity does not prove requirements correct or authenticate input observations.

title: Model checking
held: explore reachable states against a property
body: Specify initial states, transitions, and a property. Explore reachable behavior and return a counterexample when a violation is found.
cost: Independent variables can make the state space grow exponentially.
example: Check that exclusive ownership is never granted twice.
mistake: A model guarantee depends on correspondence to deployment.

title: SAT and SMT
held: ask whether a logical formula has a satisfying assignment
body: SAT handles Boolean formulas; SMT adds theories such as bitvectors and arithmetic. A satisfying assignment is a witness in that model.
cost: General SAT is NP-complete; theory fragments have different costs.
example: Equivalence can be checked by searching for an input with differing outputs.
mistake: Timeout and unknown are not unsatisfiability.

title: Tau Language
held: express behavior as logical requirements in Tau
body: Tau expresses executable logical specifications. This experiment exports tables as Boolean equations and compares actual Tau 0.8 outputs with an independent evaluator.
cost: Preparation cost depends on specification size and algebra.
example: XOR is expressed as out[t] = a[t] ^ b[t].
mistake: Runtime agreement establishes correspondence on checked inputs, not prediction accuracy.

title: ZenoFCIS
held: qualify a candidate implementation with a contract checker
body: Separate candidate construction from acceptance by a named checker over a declared domain. Record source identity and replayable evidence.
cost: Cost depends on domain, checker, and representation.
example: Exhaustively compare implementations over a bounded domain.
mistake: Proposal, checked acceptance, and deployment are different events.

title: Layered lookup tables
held: compose small learned truth tables into a bigger function
body: Each unit stores a small finite function. Composition exploits structure without storing every whole-input case. Training selects entries; frozen inference is deterministic.
cost: Two-input Boolean tables have four entries; evaluation is linear in visited tables.
example: This companion uses frozen Boolean tables to route text.
mistake: Representability does not guarantee compactness, easy learning, or broad language ability.

title: Circuit folding
held: remove redundant gates while preserving observable outputs
body: Propagate constants, absorb negations, bypass wires, share equal computations, and remove dead nodes. Preserve output votes and polarities.
cost: Graph simplification can reduce runtime work.
example: x OR 0 can be replaced by x.
mistake: Equal final labels on samples are weaker than preservation of every vote.

title: Q learning
held: learn state action values from rewards
body: A Q table estimates future return per state-action pair. Updates combine observed reward with an estimate of next-state value.
cost: Storage grows with states times actions.
example: A finite grid policy learns useful moves.
mistake: Estimated reward is not a safety guarantee outside the modeled environment.

title: Safety guards
held: reject or repair a learned action that breaks a checked rule
body: A learned policy proposes an action; a separately specified guard accepts, rejects, or replaces it. State the guard's scope and fallback.
cost: Cost depends on the rule and state representation.
example: A game guard rejects moves onto occupied squares.
mistake: Local legality does not prove a long-term objective like never losing.

title: Deterministic inference
held: get the same output from the same frozen inputs
body: Fixed tables, input normalization, and tie-breaking give repeatable integer inference. Floating-point training can still depend on libraries and execution order.
cost: Frozen inference performs bounded graph work.
example: Same message, context, and model bytes must give the same trace.
mistake: A random seed alone does not guarantee cross-platform identical training.

title: Verification and accuracy
held: distinguish faithful execution from good predictions
body: A model can execute exactly and choose the wrong answer. Measure prediction quality on held-out inputs and implementation correspondence separately.
cost: Different measurements answer different questions.
example: An always-zero classifier can be perfectly implemented and mostly inaccurate.
mistake: Parity is not proof of relevant or correct conversation.

title: Capabilities and limits
held: describe the small local chat experiment
body: I am a bounded local companion for algorithms and formal methods. Learned tables choose topics, authored cards supply prose, and deterministic tools calculate examples.
cost: Local integer inference; no remote language model.
example: Try sorting, shortest paths, knapsack, edit distance, GCD, or method comparisons.
mistake: Synthetic training volume is not evidence of general conversation ability.

title: Hello
held: greet the algorithm companion
body: Hello. Ask about algorithms or layered tables, compare two methods, or run a small example with a trace.
cost: All chat computation runs in this browser.
example: Try 'gcd 1071 462' or 'what is dynamic programming?'.
mistake: Ambiguous questions may need a more specific topic.

title: Thanks
held: acknowledge a useful explanation
body: You're welcome. Try another example, ask about complexity, or compare with a different method.
cost: No remote inference is needed.
example: Ask 'compare BFS and Dijkstra'.
mistake: The learned topic route can be wrong.

title: Outside the catalog
held: ask something outside this bounded catalog
body: I do not have a reliable answer in this catalog. I can help with algorithms, formal methods, layered tables, and the commands in Help.
cost: No web access or general language model is connected.
example: Try a named algorithm or a command from Help.
mistake: The largest score alone does not mean a question is in scope.
